t: 3690. Split and Merge Array Transformation — Editorial
o:
## Understanding the problem
One operation: cut out any contiguous subarray of nums1 and reinsert it (order preserved) anywhere in the remainder. Transform nums1 into nums2 in minimum operations. n ≤ 6, so the state space is at most 6! = 720 permutations — unweighted shortest path = BFS over permutations.

Example 1 needs 1 move ([3] to the back); example 2 needs 3 moves as demonstrated.
k: States are permutations; each operation generates O(n³) successors (O(n²) cuts × O(n) insertion slots).
BFS guarantees minimality since every operation costs 1.
720 states × ~216 successors keeps the search trivial.

a.i: From each dequeued permutation, enumerate every (L, R) cut, splice out the block, and try every insertion position, enqueueing unseen tuples at distance + 1. Stop when nums2 is generated (or dequeued).
s: Start BFS from tuple(nums1); if equal to target return 0.
For each state, for each L ≤ R: remove block, reinsert at each valid position.
Return distance when target first appears; unreachable is impossible here (any permutation is reachable).
a.t: O(P · n³) with P ≤ 720 permutations — each state expands O(n²) cuts × O(n) insertions.
a.sp: O(P · n) for the distance map and queue.

w: BFS is clearly sufficient at n ≤ 6; bidirectional BFS would roughly halve the branching if n were slightly larger. Pitfalls: forgetting insertion at the very front/end (loop p to rest.length inclusive), and hashing arrays properly in Java/JS. Follow-up: prove every permutation is reachable, or generalize to n ≤ 9 with meet-in-the-middle.
